newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin aims to buttress reform with bold shake-up.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin aims to buttress reform with bold shake-up.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin's decision on Tuesday to order a complete overhaul of his government shows his top priority now is saving his economic reforms to secure his place in history, analysts said.
A presidential decree has in effect given Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and his new first deputy, the unpopular liberal Anatoly Chubais, carte blanche to form a new cabinet.

The order followed a robust state-of-the-nation speech in which Yeltsin, newly recovered from heart surgery and pneumonia, vowed to restore order, weed out corruption and revive Russia's stagnant economy.
"With this decree Yeltsin hopes to secure his place in the history books in the three or so years that remain to him," said Andrei Piontkovsky, head of the Centre for Strategic Studies.
"This reshuffle is the last chance for democratic market reforms in Russia this century."

Dogged by health problems, Yeltsin has been mostly absent from the Kremlin since being re-elected for a second term last July. His many critics say he lacks the energy and vision to lead his vast country to the year 2000 when his mandate ends.
But in his speech to parliament last week, Yeltsin made clear he was back at the helm and intended to take bold action.
"Enough is enough...The time has come to restore order and I will do that," he said.
"The structure and composition of the government must be changed. Energetic and competent people will come," Yeltsin said, looking ahead to his cabinet overhaul.

"In 2000 Russia will elect a new president. I want to pass on to my successor a country with a dynamically growing economy, an effective and fair social protection system, a country whose people look to the future with confidence."
Yeltsin's decree puts all cabinet jobs except Chernomyrdin's and, by implication, Chubais', up for grabs and also demands big cuts in the government's bloated bureaucracy.

"The mood of the whole government and its behaviour will become more aggressive, more focused on achieving real economic results after these changes," said political analyst Irina Kobrinskaya of the Carnegie Endownment for International Peace think-tank.
"The next few months will be hard for Yeltsin and the government," she added.
Chubais, expected to be in control of economic reforms, and whatever new team is formed will have to act quickly to defuse mounting social tensions and revive the struggling economy.

The opposition-dominated State Duma lower house of parliament has thrown its weight behind a nationwide general strike set for March 27 to protest against non-payment of wages and pensions to millions of impoverished Russians.

The communists are threatening a no-confidence motion in the new government which, if voted through twice, would pose Yeltsin with the choice of dismissing the cabinet or the Duma itself. A fresh election might return an even less cooperative Duma.

But the appointment of Chubais, youthful mastermind of Russia's controversial privatisation programme, shows Yeltsin, 66, has not lost his love of a good fight. Chubais is hated by many ordinary people and opposition leaders who accuse him of channelling Russia's wealth into the hands of a few.
"Appointing him first deputy prime minister is to spit at public opinion," said the popular Moscow daily Moskovsky Komsomolets on Tuesday in a caustic front-page article.
However Chubais is admired in the West for his economic views and some Russian liberals see his promotion as the last chance for the country's market reforms.
"The old government had to go. It is a coalition of feudal clans fighting for access to state budget resources," Piontkovsky told Reuters.
"They are not interested in market reforms but in perpetuating the status quo of cosy ties between politics and big business," he said.
